pluss::note::bytes¶

Back to Note Factory API Reference

Signatures¶

Note pluss::note::bytes(text_source values)
Note pluss::note::bytes(string_range flat, integer_range sizes)
Note pluss::note::bytes(byte_range raw)

Raw Byte Content, No UTF-8 Assumption¶

bytes() builds a Note in bytes mode (encoding=bytes). It is the right constructor whenever the content is not guaranteed to be well-formed text: binary blobs, protocol frames, hashes, encrypted payloads, arbitrary file contents, or text in an unknown or mixed encoding.

The difference from make is a contract, not a storage change. Both keep the exact bytes you give them. But a UTF-8-mode Note promises its cells are text and lets text methods (character length, case mapping, regex, tokenization) act on them; a bytes-mode Note makes no such promise, and its printer shows the bytes rather than pretending they render as characters. Convert a bytes Note to text explicitly once you know the encoding is safe.

bytes() accepts the same call-site spellings as make() — a scalar, a braced list, a nested block up to rank 3, or a contiguous range of strings — plus one form make() does not have:

  • byte_range raw — a contiguous range of std::byte read as one opaque scalar cell. Use this for a buffer that is genuinely a single blob, including one that contains embedded NUL bytes.

The (flat, sizes) overload works exactly as it does for make(): the flat cell count must equal the product of sizes.

Printing bytes¶

pluss::note::print shows a bytes-mode Note with a b"..." marker by default (NotePrintBytesMode::Escaped). Printable ASCII is shown as-is; every other byte — controls, DEL, and everything >= 0x80 — is written as a \xNN escape, so the escaped view is always plain ASCII and safe to paste into text. Set opt.bytes_mode = pluss::NotePrintBytesMode::Hex for a hex[..] byte grid instead — the same information without the \x noise when almost nothing is printable.

A C++ string-literal caveat¶

bytes({"\x00\x01\x02"}) does not store three bytes: a C string literal ends at its first NUL, so "\x00..." is an empty string before it ever reaches bytes(). To carry embedded NULs, use the byte_range overload (Example 5) or a std::string with an explicit length. This is a property of C++ literals, not of bytes().

Example 1: A Scalar Of ASCII Bytes¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(pluss::note::bytes("plain ascii bytes")) << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=bytes)
b"plain ascii bytes"

Same bytes as pluss::note::make("plain ascii bytes") would hold — but encoding=bytes and the b"..." marker signal “not promised to be text”.

Example 2: A One-Dimensional Batch (Default Escaped Print)¶

const pluss::Note n = pluss::note::bytes({"AB", "\xDE\xAD\xBE\xEF"});
std::cout << n << "\n";  // operator<< == print() with default options

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=bytes)
[b"AB", b"\xDE\xAD\xBE\xEF"]

AB is printable so it shows literally; DE AD BE EF are non-ASCII bytes, so the escaped printer writes each as a \xNN escape rather than emitting raw bytes. The next example shows the same value as a hex grid.

Example 3: The Same Value, Hex Dump¶

pluss::NotePrintOptions hex;
hex.bytes_mode = pluss::NotePrintBytesMode::Hex;
std::cout << pluss::note::print(pluss::note::bytes({"AB", "\xDE\xAD\xBE\xEF"}), hex)
          << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=bytes)
[hex[41 42], hex[de ad be ef]]

hex[..] shows every byte unambiguously. Prefer it whenever the content is not mostly printable.

Example 4: Flat Storage Plus An Explicit Shape¶

std::vector<std::string> flat{"one", "two", "three", "four"};
std::array<std::int64_t, 2> sizes{2, 2};
const pluss::Note n = pluss::note::bytes(
    pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string>(flat),
    pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::int64_t>(sizes));
pluss::note::print(std::cout, n) << "\n";  // print(os, n) returns the stream

Output¶

Note(shape=[2, 2], dim=2, numel=4, encoding=bytes)
[
  [b"one", b"two"], 
  [b"three", b"four"]
]

Example 5: A Raw std::byte Buffer As One Scalar¶

std::array<std::byte, 4> raw{std::byte{0x48}, std::byte{0x69},
                             std::byte{0x21}, std::byte{0x00}};
const pluss::Note n = pluss::note::bytes(
    pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::byte>(raw));
std::cout << n << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=bytes)
b"Hi!\x00"

The whole range is one cell, and the trailing NUL is kept — unlike a C string literal, which would have stopped at it. The same value as a hex dump:

std::cout << pluss::note::print(n, hex) << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=bytes)
hex[48 69 21 00]

Example 6: The String-Literal NUL Caveat, Shown¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(pluss::note::bytes({"\x00\x01\x02", "kept"}), hex)
          << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=bytes)
[hex[], hex[6b 65 70 74]]

The first cell is empty — "\x00\x01\x02" is a zero-length C literal. The second cell is fine (kept = 6b 65 70 74). Reach for the byte_range overload when NULs must survive.

Example 7: Escaped Vs Hex On The Same Cells¶

const pluss::Note n = pluss::note::bytes({"\xC3\xA9", "\xFF"});
std::cout << pluss::note::print(n) << "\n";        // default: escaped
std::cout << pluss::note::print(n, hex) << "\n";   // hex

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=bytes)
[b"\xC3\xA9", b"\xFF"]
Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=bytes)
[hex[c3 a9], hex[ff]]

In a bytes-mode Note every non-ASCII byte is escaped, so C3 A9 (which would be é as UTF-8 text) and the lone FF both show as \x escapes — the printer does not try to decode them. The hex view is the same bytes in lower-case without the \x. Contrast make, where a UTF-8-mode Note holding those same C3 A9 bytes prints as é.

See Also¶

  • pluss::note::make: the UTF-8-mode constructor — use it when the content is known-good text.

  • pluss::note::full_bytes_like / pluss::note::empty_bytes_like: shape-first bytes-mode construction from an existing Note.

  • pluss::note::print: the renderer and its bytes_mode option.
